html:
A Finno-Ugric people of the far northeast of European Russia, along the Vychegda, Pechora and upper Kama rivers. On the map in 1530 their label sits just east of the Urals, in the Ob basin; their homeland is west of the mountains, though Komi hunters and traders crossed them often.

The Komi descend from the Permian peoples of the forest north. In the 1370s and 1380s the missionary Stephen of Perm converted many of them and made the Old Permic script to write their language. Their lands paid tribute first to Novgorod and then to Moscow, which absorbed them fully by the late 15th century as the Russian state grew.

Komi were skilled hunters, fishers and fur traders. They guided and joined Russian expeditions over the Urals into Siberia, and some later took up reindeer herding from the Nenets. Their language, close to Udmurt, is still spoken in the Komi Republic.
